title: Identifying a model from input and output records

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: An output that rises smoothly and levels off.
sections.body_md:
System identification turns input and output records into a model. The model in this skill is linear in its parameters, so the fit is a least-squares problem. A first-order plant is the running example: one number for the DC gain and one number for the time constant. The same arithmetic fits any model you can write as \(y = \Phi \theta\), with a regressor \(\Phi\) built from the records.

A step that has settled is enough for the gain. It is a poor instrument for a fast pole, which can vanish before your samples start. A frequency sweep sees that pole as a change in magnitude and phase. Either way, the residual and a held-out record decide whether the model is any good.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
A line through the origin, \(y = \theta u\), has the scalar normal equation \(\theta = \sum uy / \sum u^2\). With several parameters the same statement is \(\Phi^T \Phi \theta = \Phi^T y\). The magnitude of a one-pole model \(k/(\tau s + 1)\) is
\[
\frac{k}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega \tau)^2}}.
\]
The residual on a sample is the measured output minus the model's prediction. A held-out record is a set of rows that were not used to choose \(\theta\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A candidate model has gain 1.8. On a fresh input of 3.5 it predicts \(1.8 \cdot 3.5 = 6.3\). The measured output on that same input is 6.45, so the residual is \(6.45 - 6.3 = 0.15\). That one sample is small beside the prediction, which is encouraging, and it is not a proof. A second held-out record with a residual that is large and shaped like the input would still reject the gain.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Inverting the normal equation, \(\sum u^2 / \sum uy\), returns the reciprocal of the gain. Averaging the ratios \(y/u\) is a different estimator from the least-squares formula. Reading a time constant from a step that has not settled mixes the unknown gain into the slope. And a small residual on the fitting record does not protect you from a fast pole the experiment never excited. The data matrix in this skill is \(\Phi\). It is not the state matrix of a realization.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A batch fit freezes \(\theta\) when the records end. An adaptive law keeps the same linear parameterization and updates \(\theta\) as new samples arrive, using the residual as the driving signal. The experiment design does not go away. If the regressor never sees a mode, the update cannot invent it.
